abstract:
Chronic liver inflammation provides a major biological context for hepatocarcinogenesis, and macrophages link innate immune sensing, fibrogenesis, immune suppression and therapeutic resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), Kupffer cells and inflammation-associated myeloid populations have been extensively investigated in HCC; however, the intellectual structure and thematic connectivity of this inflammation-centered research field remain incompletely defined.
This study aimed to map the intellectual architecture, evolutionary trajectory and inter-module connectivity of inflammation-centered macrophage research in HCC using bibliometric and scientometric methods.
A total of 9218 English-language articles and reviews on macrophage-related HCC from 2005 to 2025 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus after systematic deduplication. CiteSpace, VOSviewer and bibliometrix were used to perform co-citation clustering, reference historiographic mapping, keyword co-occurrence analysis, publication-volume-adjusted keyword correlation analysis, citation burst detection, journal dual-map overlay and multi-level collaboration profiling.
Annual publication output increased from 84 articles in 2005 to 1129 in 2025. Co-citation analysis resolved 13 well-defined clusters (modularity Q = 0.744; mean silhouette S = 0.884), and historiographic mapping identified four sequential stages: foundational inflammation and hepatocarcinogenesis, mechanistic expansion of TAM function, immune-regulatory convergence and spatial immunology. Keyword dynamics showed a transition from viral hepatitis, innate immunity, Kupffer cells and fibroinflammatory terminology toward TAM-mediated immune suppression, immunotherapy, single-cell analysis, SPP1-positive macrophage-associated spatial immune barriers and computational precision oncology. After annual publication-volume adjustment, the foundational viral-innate module and the contemporary computational-precision oncology module showed a negative inter-module Pearson correlation (mean r = -0.383), lower than expected under label-permutation and temporal-succession null models (both p < 0.001). Three low-connectivity literature interfaces emerged: etiology-immunotherapy, TAM-organized spatial immune exclusion and TAM-MDSC shared myeloid biology.
Macrophage-related HCC research has evolved from inflammation-centered hepatocarcinogenesis toward spatially resolved and computationally assisted immunology. The low-connectivity interfaces identified in this study should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating bibliometric signals rather than as evidence of biological or clinical disconnection or as stand-alone research priorities derived from network structure alone. Their potential translational relevance should be considered alongside published mechanistic and clinical evidence and requires future mechanistic, spatial and prospective clinical validation.

New ZealandJ Inflamm Res1015126841178-7031Long-term liver inflammation is an important driver of hepatocellular carcinoma. Macrophages are key immune cells that link liver injury and scarring with immune suppression and treatment resistance. Research in this area has grown rapidly, making it difficult to see how different lines of work fit together. In this study, we mapped 9218 publications on macrophage-related hepatocellular carcinoma research published between 2005 and 2025. We analyzed publication trends, research collaborations, highly cited studies, changes in research topics and links between research themes. We found that earlier studies focused on viral hepatitis, innate immune signaling and Kupffer cells, which are macrophages normally found in the liver. More recent studies increasingly focus on tumor-associated macrophages, immunotherapy, methods that study individual cells, the spatial organization of immune cells and data-driven cancer research. We also found that older inflammation-centered themes and newer data-driven or precision-cancer themes were only weakly connected in the published literature. This pattern describes how research topics are connected in publications and should not be taken as proof of a biological or clinical gap. Instead, it suggests that future studies may benefit from linking the causes of liver disease with macrophage behavior, the spatial organization of immune cells and interactions among tumor-related immune cells.
